prize_parts.citation: for formal and empirical analysis of how electoral rules, constitutions, state capacity and fiscal institutions shape policy choices and economic performance

statement.case_for: I keep B027 as a single-part configuration with Persson, Tabellini and Besley. The discovery is a common formal framework for why electoral rules, constitutional design, state capacity and fiscal institutions produce different policies and growth outcomes. Its empirical tests were later strengthened by more design-based work on local rules and accountability. The core contributions are about three decades old, so replication, extension and challenge have mostly happened. That is the main reason I weigh maturity above recency. The credit is concentrated. Persson and Tabellini are the joint core, and the Besley-Persson work on state capacity and Besley's work on political agency form a second strand that supplies the fiscal and state-capacity half of the proposed citation. I have reread the round-1 exchange and the chair's questions. The configuration is unchanged, but three things changed in how I hold it. First, I now state the common weighting explicitly: identification quality, conceptual originality, maturity and attribution tractability, each counted. On that weighting I rank B027 above B004 and B002 mainly on maturity and attribution tractability, and I put B002 above B027 on identification quality alone. Second, I have narrowed the citation so that it claims a framework and its tests, not causal settlement of every cross-country coefficient. Third, I treat the Persson-Tabellini pair as an acceptable fallback if the committee judges Besley's strand separable. I do not count the three first-place rankings for B027, or those for B002, as evidence of merit.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is identification. Much of the evidence on electoral rules and constitutions comes from cross-country comparisons with endogenous adoption, and it is less clean than the design-based work in B002 and B024. Under common criteria that is a real cost, and a committee that weights identification most heavily could reasonably prefer B002. The second reservation is thematic proximity to the 2024 institutions prize. I think the scientific content is distinct, because this work takes institutions as given and asks how rules shape policy choices. But I cannot rule out that the committee treats proximity as a timing reason to wait. The third is attribution. Besley's claim is strong but is more complementary than central to the joint Persson-Tabellini core. Any trio from a field with many prominent contributors is also contestable. Finally, no single configuration has more than three explicit supporters in round 1, so my preferred part reaches six only if others move. That is a process fact, not a scientific objection.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B002 first and B027 sixth. She argues that in B002 the empirical claims come from within-family and mover designs that can be evaluated directly. In B027 the electoral-rule findings rest on cross-country identification less clean than the theory. She also sees a boundary problem with the 2024 prize and a division of credit between theory and cross-country evidence.
responses.response: I accept the first half of your argument. On identification quality alone B002 is stronger, and I said so in round 1. Two things keep me from letting that decide the comparison. Mover and exposure designs also rest on assumptions, such as the absence of time-varying confounds at the moment of moving, and these are still being examined outside the US. A design that is more checkable is not yet a design whose long-run conclusions are settled. And a framework can be a prize-worthy discovery even where the early cross-country tests were weak. The framework generated the sharp predictions that later quasi-experimental work on local electoral rules and accountability tested. On the boundary with 2024, I read that prize as concerning the origins of institutions and long-run prosperity. B027 concerns the policy formation that institutions produce. I concede that this is a judgement the committee may weigh differently, and I treat it as timing rather than as a scientific objection.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B002 first. He argues that the Chetty-Hendren-Friedman trio is the tightest attribution and that the core results are replicated and extended with other administrative datasets. He keeps the citation close to the measurement and exposure-effect evidence. He also names maturity and the Katz question as the open issues.
responses.response: Your citation discipline is the right response to my maturity concern, and it narrows our disagreement. If B002 were framed around measurement and exposure-based designs, I would not call it premature. As a historian who builds datasets, I also take the data-construction contribution seriously. What still separates us is how much weight the long-run causal claims should get. Evidence that would move me is replication of exposure-effect estimates in non-US administrative data and long-run follow-up of the same cohorts. I would ask the committee to state which of these it treats as necessary. On attribution I agree with you that the trio is the recurring unit, and Katz is the live question. I still rank B002 as my first alternative and not as my preferred part, because B027 has three more decades of testing and a comparably tractable attribution.

responses.point: Fredriksson moved from the Persson-Tabellini pair to the trio including Besley. He argues that the state-capacity and political-selection strand is not derivative of the constitutions-and-electoral-rules work. He also says the 2024 prize should enter as a timing consideration, not a scientific one.
responses.response: I agree on the trio and on the framing of the 2024 prize, and I thank you for tying the third name to the citation. I would add one condition. If the citation names state capacity and fiscal institutions, the third name is needed to support it. If the committee prefers a citation limited to electoral rules and constitutions, the pair is sufficient and I would not object. I would not claim Besley is as central as Persson or Tabellini. My point is that the strand is separable and the citation as drafted depends on it. On your identification caveat, I weigh it as you do, as a real cost that the framework's testable predictions only partly offset.

responses.point: Strömberg ranks B004 first with Kiyotaki, Moore and Gertler. He says Kiyotaki-Moore are the clear originators, accepts that the 2022 prize overlaps with the accelerator strand, and keeps Gertler for the later intermediary-finance work with Kiyotaki. He lists B027 as an alternative because of its concentrated credit.
responses.response: I take your Gertler argument more seriously than I did in round 1. Separating intermediary balance-sheet work from the Bernanke-Gertler accelerator is a real distinction. It leaves me thinking that the committee's open question is a pair or a trio, and that Kiyotaki-Moore is the clean fallback. You and I are therefore in a similar position, each with a clean core and a contested third name. That symmetry means neither of us should treat the third name as decisive. Where we still differ is on marginal novelty. For B004 I accept your point that the 2008 crisis tested the mechanism, but I give weight to the fact that the 2022 prize covers adjacent ground more directly than the 2024 prize covers B027. That is why I keep B004 as an alternative and not as the preferred part. I also note that aggregate evidence for the mechanism is more indirect than the firm and household evidence you cite, which makes the comparison with B027's cross-country identification closer than either of us may want.

responses.point: Teorell ranks B027 first. He says Besley's claim is complementary rather than central, and he would accept the Persson-Tabellini pair as a fallback. He distinguishes the 2024 prize on the origins of institutions from this work on policy choice, and he discloses that he delivered the 2024 presentation speech.
responses.response: I agree with your distinction and with the fallback. I also share your caution. You gave the 2024 speech, and I gave the 2023 speech, so neither of us should treat our own reading of what an adjacent prize covered as independent evidence. Presentation speeches do not establish private preferences, and I would not count our agreement as corroboration. I would test the distinction against the content of the citations. A 2026 citation on electoral rules, constitutions and state capacity does not restate a 2024 citation on colonial origins and persistence. I differ slightly on Besley. I read his strand as separable and needed for the state-capacity half of the citation, and I accept that this is a judgement. If the committee votes on the pair in a later step, I would not treat that as a loss of the discovery.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats the 2024 institutions prize as bearing on novelty or only on timing, and how much weight proximity should carry against the distinct content of policy-making and electoral-rules research.
Whether the best attribution is the Persson-Tabellini pair or the trio with Besley, and whether the state-capacity strand is separable enough that the citation would lose something without it.
How much weaker cross-country identification should count against B027 relative to the design-based evidence in B002, and whether later quasi-experimental work carries enough of the empirical case.

Whether B002 will be judged mature enough on its measurement and exposure designs alone. My ranking is sensitive to this, and evidence from non-US administrative data or long-run follow-up could move it above B027.

Whether Kiyotaki and Moore alone (B004) would be a cleaner attribution than any trio on the table. I have not resolved whether the 2022 overlap with that agenda outweighs the overlap I face with 2024.
My assessments rely on general knowledge of the literature and the supplied round-1 files, not independent verification of citations, replication results or priority claims.
statement.conflict_note: No co-authorship or institutional tie to Persson, Tabellini or Besley appears in my supplied profile. My co-authored work with political scientist Johannes Lindvall and Alexandra Cermeño on railroads and the nation state is topically adjacent to the state-capacity literature, and I disclose that adjacency. Tommy Andersson is a Lund colleague on the committee and Jan Teorell was formerly at Lund; I have no stated co-authorship with either and I do not treat that as evidence for or against any candidate. My round-1 note referred to Persson's past committee service. I can only take that from a colleague's disclosure as recorded in the chair summary, and my profile adds nothing to it. I presented the 2023 speech and the 2025 press conference for the Academy. These do not establish private preferences, and I do not know whether I drafted the corresponding Scientific Backgrounds. As a historian who builds datasets, I may be sympathetic to the data-construction contribution in B002, which I have tried to weigh equally with B027. This is a disclosure only and not a recusal.
